theoryMore:
**Pieces the questions use.** `Button("Save") { save() }` takes the title and, in the trailing closure, the action that runs on tap. When the label needs to be more than text, use `Button(action: save) { Label("Save", systemImage: "tray") }`: the `action:` closure does the work and the `label:` closure draws the button. `Label` combines a title and an icon and adapts to its context (list, toolbar, button). Icons come from two places: `Image("photo")` looks up a file in the project's Asset Catalog, and `Image(systemName: "star")` uses an SF Symbol, a vector icon from the system that follows the font weight and can be colored with `.foregroundStyle(.yellow)`.

**Order matters for every modifier, not just padding.** `Text("A").frame(width: 100).background(.blue)` paints an area 100 points wide, because `frame` creates a container view of that size and the background is applied to it. `Text("A").background(.blue).frame(width: 100)` paints only the text and leaves the rest of the frame transparent. Rule: each modifier acts on the result of everything that came before it.

**@ViewBuilder outside body.** `@ViewBuilder` is a result builder: it lets you write several views, `if` and `switch` without `return`. `body` gets it by default, but you can apply it to your own functions and properties:
`@ViewBuilder func badge(_ ok: Bool) -> some View { if ok { Image(systemName: "checkmark") } else { Text("Pending") } }`
Without it, the two branches of the `if` would have different types, and `some View` (a single concrete type) would not compile. It also works on parameters of container views, as in `struct Card<Content: View>: View { @ViewBuilder var content: Content; var body: some View { VStack { content }.padding() } }`, which lets you write `Card { Text("a"); Text("b") }`.

**A reusable style with native modifier syntax.** After creating `struct Highlight: ViewModifier`, you can apply it with `.modifier(Highlight())`. To call just `.highlight()`, add `extension View { func highlight() -> some View { modifier(Highlight()) } }`. This is only ergonomics: the result is identical.

**Identity, state and the role of body.** SwiftUI ties '@State' to the view's position in the hierarchy. The two branches of an `if` are different views: when a branch leaves the screen, the view and its state are discarded, and when it returns it starts from scratch. To preserve state, move it to an ancestor (one that does not switch branches) or hide the view with `.opacity(show ? 1 : 0)` instead of using `if`. Because SwiftUI calls `body` many times, it must be fast and only describe the interface from the state. Network and disk writes belong in `.task`, `.onAppear` or button actions (more in the 'Animations, Gestures and Presentations' pillar). Splitting a screen into small subviews is cheap (they are lightweight structs) and helps the framework re-evaluate only the subviews whose inputs changed.

**Grids: the `columns` parameter.** In `LazyVGrid(columns: [GridItem(.flexible()), GridItem(.flexible())]) { ... }`, the `columns:` parameter takes an array of `GridItem`, and each element describes one column: so this example creates 2 columns that split the width equally. `.fixed(100)` creates a 100-point column, `.flexible()` a column that stretches, and `.adaptive(minimum: 80)` fits as many columns as will fit, each at least 80 points wide. Rows appear on their own as the `ForEach` items arrive. A vertical grid scrolls, so use it inside a `ScrollView`. Its horizontal version, `LazyHGrid`, uses the `rows:` parameter. `Grid { GridRow { Text("a"); Text("b") } }` creates all cells at once and aligns rows and columns like a table; use it for a few cells with precise alignment.

**Alignment.** `VStack(alignment: .leading)` aligns the children to the leading edge on the horizontal axis (the default for `VStack` is `.center`). `leading` and `trailing` flip in right-to-left languages, unlike `left` and `right`. In `ZStack(alignment: .bottomTrailing)`, the corner is matched on both axes.

**`fixedSize` and priority.** `fixedSize(horizontal:vertical:)` says, for each axis, whether the view should use its ideal size instead of the proposed size. `Text(long).fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true)` keeps the width proposed by the parent and lets the text grow in height, without truncating. `layoutPriority(1)` on a child of an `HStack` makes that child receive space before the others when space is short:
`HStack { Text(title).layoutPriority(1); Text(subtitle) }`.

**`overlay` and `background`.** `Text("x").padding().background(.yellow).overlay(alignment: .topTrailing) { Circle().frame(width: 8) }` draws the circle on top and the yellow underneath. Neither changes the size of the base view, unlike a `ZStack`, which grows to fit all its children. They are ideal for badges and borders.

**Adapting and custom layouts.** `@Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) private var sc` is `.compact` or `.regular`; choose the structure with `if sc == .compact { VStack { ... } } else { HStack { ... } }`. Size classes describe the available space, not the device model. To build your own container, adopt the `Layout` protocol and implement two methods: `sizeThatFits(proposal:subviews:cache:)` reports the container's size, and `placeSubviews(in:proposal:subviews:cache:)` positions each child with `subview.place(at:proposal:)`.

**A fixed Binding for previews.** `Child(count: .constant(3))` creates a Binding that always holds 3, useful in `#Preview` when there is no real '@State' to bind to.

**Lifting state up.** If two sibling views need the same data, it should not live in either of them: move it to the common ancestor, which becomes the owner (`@State private var count = 0`), and hand the children a Binding (`Child(count: $count)`). A child with `var count: Int` receives only a copy, so `count += 1` does not compile; with `@Binding var count: Int` it writes to the parent's data.

**`@Observable` model: owner and consumer.** The owner keeps the instance in '@State': `@State private var profile = Profile()`. This is needed because the view's struct is recreated often; without '@State', each recreation would run `Profile()` again and lose the data. A view that receives the model as a parameter and must edit it with controls uses `@Bindable var profile: Profile`, which enables `TextField("Name", text: $profile.name)`. If it only reads the value, a plain property is enough.

**Environment: models and custom keys.** To share a model without passing it through every initializer: the ancestor calls `.environment(profile)` and whoever needs it reads with `@Environment(Profile.self) var profile`. For a value of your own (a theme, for example), create a key that adopts `EnvironmentKey`, which requires a static `defaultValue` (used when no ancestor injected anything), and expose it in an extension of `EnvironmentValues`:
`private struct ThemeKey: EnvironmentKey { static let defaultValue = Theme() }`
`extension EnvironmentValues { var theme: Theme { get { self[ThemeKey.self] } set { self[ThemeKey.self] = newValue } } }`
Then inject with `.environment(\.theme, Theme(name: "dark"))` and read with `@Environment(\.theme) var theme`. In Swift 6, use `static let` for the `defaultValue`. Since Xcode 16, the `@Entry` macro writes all of this for you: `extension EnvironmentValues { @Entry var theme = Theme() }`.

**Legacy style.** With `ObservableObject`, the model is a class with `@Published` properties: `final class Cart: ObservableObject { @Published var items: [String] = [] }`. The view that creates the object declares it with `@StateObject private var cart = Cart()`, which keeps the same instance across updates. A view that merely receives an object created elsewhere uses `@ObservedObject var cart: Cart`. If you created the object with `@ObservedObject` inside the view, it would be recreated and lose its data. In the legacy style, any changed `@Published` re-evaluates every observing view; with '@Observable', only the views that read the changed property.

**Identity in lists.** An `Identifiable` type has a stable `id` property: `struct Task: Identifiable { let id = UUID(); var title: String }`. With it, write `List(tasks) { t in Text(t.title) }`. If the type is not `Identifiable`, give the identifier path: `List(names, id: \.self) { Text($0) }`, where `\.self` uses the value itself (which must be `Hashable`).

**Deleting, moving and grouping.** `onDelete` and `onMove` are applied to the `ForEach`, not to the `List` or to the rows. The delete closure receives an `IndexSet` with the positions to remove, and the move closure receives that set and the destination:
`ForEach(tasks) { t in Text(t.title) }`
`.onDelete { tasks.remove(atOffsets: $0) }`
`.onMove { tasks.move(fromOffsets: $0, toOffset: $1) }`
For the drag handles to appear, the list must be in edit mode; the simplest way is an `EditButton()` in the toolbar. You update the array yourself; SwiftUI only tells you what the user did. `Section("Pending") { ForEach(...) }` groups rows with an optional header and footer.

**Navigation stack from code.** `NavigationPath` is a stack of `Hashable` values that can mix different types (a `[Task]` array accepts only one type). Push with `path.append(task)` and go back to the root with `path.removeLast(path.count)`. There is no `clear()` method. The environment action `dismiss()` only closes the current screen; it does not empty the stack. Each pushed type needs its own `.navigationDestination(for: Task.self) { t in DetailView(task: t) }`, declared inside the `NavigationStack`. A `NavigationLink(value: task)` is decoupled from the destination, which is created only when needed; `NavigationLink(destination:)` builds and fixes the destination view at the link's location. The title (`.navigationTitle`) and the bar (`.toolbar`) belong to the content view.

**Search and refresh.** `.searchable(text: $query)` only shows the field and binds the text; the filter is yours: `var filtered: [Task] { query.isEmpty ? tasks : tasks.filter { $0.title.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(query) } }`. `.refreshable { await reload() }` takes an `async` closure, and the loading indicator stays visible until it finishes.

**Tabs and columns.** From iOS 18: `TabView { Tab("Home", systemImage: "house") { HomeView() } }` (before, `.tabItem { }` on each view). `NavigationSplitView { Sidebar() } detail: { Detail() }` builds two or three columns, which collapse into a stack on iPhone.

**Avoid `ForEach(0..<tasks.count)` with mutable data:** the range is computed once and can point to indices that no longer exist when the array shrinks. Use `ForEach(tasks)` with a stable identity.

**Exact types in Bindings.** `Slider` edits a floating-point number. In `@State var volume = 5`, the literal `5` becomes `Int`, and `Slider(value: $volume, in: 0...10)` does not compile. Declare `@State var volume: Double = 5` (or `= 5.0`). The same care applies to `Picker`: it compares each option's `tag` with the selection, type by type. If the selection is optional (`@State var color: Hue?`), the tags must also be optional: `Text("Blue").tag(Hue?.some(.blue))` and, for the empty option, `Text("None").tag(Hue?.none)`. With `.tag(Hue.blue)` the selection is never recognized. The style changes with `.pickerStyle(.segmented)` (a few short options, 2 to 4), `.menu`, `.wheel` or `.navigationLink`.

**Focus and keyboard.** `@FocusState private var field: Field?` stores which field is active, using an enum of fields: `enum Field { case email, password }`. Each control declares its value: `TextField("Email", text: $email).focused($field, equals: .email)`. To move focus, assign: `field = .password`. `submitLabel(.next)` changes the Return key's text (`.done`, `.search`...), and `onSubmit { field = .password }` runs when it is tapped. `keyboardType(.emailAddress)` picks the keyboard and `textContentType(.password)` helps autofill.

**Role, validation and other controls.** `Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { remove() }` only indicates the meaning (usually shown in red, and accessibility gets the information too); deleting is still the job of your closure. To block submission with an empty field, derive the condition from state: `Button("Send") { send() }.disabled(email.isEmpty)`. `DatePicker("Date", selection: $date, displayedComponents: .date)` shows only the date (use `.hourAndMinute` for time, or both). `TextEditor(text: $text)` edits multiple lines and has no built-in placeholder. `Link("Site", destination: url)` opens a URL; `ShareLink(item: url)` opens the system share sheet.

**SecureField and accessibility.** `SecureField` merely masks the characters on screen: it encrypts nothing, and storing passwords is the Keychain's job. Standard controls are already accessible: the title (`Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $enabled)`) becomes the VoiceOver label, and the on or off state is announced. An icon-only button needs an explicit label: `Button { } label: { Image(systemName: "trash") }.accessibilityLabel("Delete")`.

**Gestures: `onChanged`, `onEnded` and `@GestureState`.** A gesture is a sequence of events. In `DragGesture().onChanged { v in offset = v.translation }.onEnded { _ in offset = .zero }`, the first closure runs on every change while the finger moves, and the second once on release. `@GestureState private var drag = CGSize.zero` stores a temporary value: you update it with `.updating($drag) { value, state, _ in state = value.translation }` and it returns by itself to the initial value when the gesture ends or is cancelled. To keep the result, copy it to a '@State' in `onEnded`. Attach a gesture with `.gesture(...)`. `LongPressGesture().sequenced(before: DragGesture())` only lets the drag begin after the long press, `simultaneously(with:)` recognizes both at the same time, and `exclusively(before:)` prefers the first. `MagnifyGesture` (pinch) delivers `value.magnification` to adjust the scale.

**Animation.** `.animation(.spring(duration: 0.5, bounce: 0), value: big)` animates the view's changes when `big` changes; `bounce: 0` means a spring with no overshoot. `withAnimation(.easeInOut) { open.toggle() }` animates everything that depends on the state changed inside the block. A `transition` (for example `.transition(.slide)`) only animates if the view enters or leaves inside an animation; without `withAnimation` or `.animation(_:value:)`, it appears and disappears with no effect. For the same view to appear to move between two layouts, declare `@Namespace private var ns` and use `matchedGeometryEffect(id: "photo", in: ns)` on both versions, with the same id and the same namespace.

**Presentations.** All of them depend on state. `.sheet(isPresented: $open) { DetailView() }` uses a Bool. `.sheet(item: $selected) { t in DetailView(task: t) }` uses an optional `Identifiable`: the content receives the value, and the Binding goes back to `nil` on close. `fullScreenCover` covers the whole screen and cannot be swiped away, so the view itself must close with `dismiss()`. Inside the presented view, `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss` followed by `dismiss()` closes it. `.presentationDetents([.medium, .large])` goes on the sheet's content view and defines the allowed heights. `alert` informs or asks for a short confirmation; `confirmationDialog` offers several actions (Save, Discard, Cancel with `role: .cancel`). On iPhone, a `popover` becomes a sheet by default; `.presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)` keeps the bubble.

**Lifecycle.** `.onAppear { }` runs when the view appears. `.task { await load() }` accepts `await` directly and the task is cancelled automatically when the view disappears (with `.onAppear { Task { } }` you would have to cancel by hand); `.task(id: value)` restarts when the value changes.

**Outlet and action in practice.** An outlet is a property that points to a storyboard object so you can read or change its properties: `@IBOutlet weak var titleLabel: UILabel!`. An action is a method that the storyboard calls when an event happens, and it receives the object that triggered it as `sender`: `@IBAction func send(_ sender: UIButton) { sender.setTitle("Sent", for: .normal) }`. If you want to change the button's title elsewhere in the code (not only inside the action), you also need an outlet for it. Having only the action does not give you a stored reference to the button.

**Why an outlet's type can be `UIView`.** Every visual element in UIKit (`UILabel`, `UIButton`, `UIImageView`, `UITextField`...) inherits from `UIView`. That is why `@IBOutlet weak var card: UIView!` accepts any of these views, while a more specific type (such as `UILabel`) gives access to its own properties (`text`, `font`). Use the most specific type you need.

**Why `weak`.** The view hierarchy already keeps a strong reference to each subview. The outlet merely points to it, so `weak` avoids unnecessary retention. The `!` (implicitly unwrapped optional) is used because the value is `nil` until the view is loaded: accessing the outlet before that, or without a connection, ends in 'Unexpectedly found nil'.

**Linking the scene to its class.** A scene only finds its outlets and actions if its controller is your Swift class. In the Identity inspector, fill the Class field with the type name (for example `ProfileViewController`). Without it, the connection has nowhere to attach. Control-dragging into code only works properly after this step.

**Broken connections.** The storyboard stores the method or property name as text. If you delete `send` from the code and leave the connection, tapping the button causes 'unrecognized selector'. If you delete a property connected to an outlet, the crash is 'not key value coding-compliant'. The fix is to remove the old connection in the Connections inspector. To rename safely, use Editor > Refactor > Rename, which also updates the storyboard.

**`@IBDesignable` and `@IBInspectable`.** `@IBDesignable class CardView: UIView { @IBInspectable var radius: CGFloat = 8 { didSet { layer.cornerRadius = radius } } }`. The first attribute (on the class) makes Interface Builder draw the view on the canvas. The second (on properties) shows them in the Attributes inspector so you can edit them without code.

**Anchors and constraints in code.** Every view has anchors (`topAnchor`, `bottomAnchor`, `leadingAnchor`, `trailingAnchor`, `centerXAnchor`, `centerYAnchor`, `widthAnchor`, `heightAnchor`), and a constraint relates one anchor to another on the same axis: `label.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.topAnchor, constant: 8)`. Mixing axes (for example `topAnchor` with `centerXAnchor`) is not allowed. To center horizontally: `view.centerXAnchor.constraint(equalTo: superview.centerXAnchor)`. Created constraints do nothing until activated, and the recommended way is to activate several at once:
`label.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false`
`NSLayoutConstraint.activate([`
`label.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.topAnchor, constant: 8),`
`label.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.leadingAnchor, constant: 16)])`
If you do not turn off `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints`, the system creates extra constraints from the frame, which fight yours.

**Safe area.** `let guide = view.safeAreaLayoutGuide` is a layout guide (an invisible rectangle) that excludes the notch, the Dynamic Island, the status bar and the home indicator. Anchor texts and buttons to its anchors (`guide.topAnchor`), and let only backgrounds reach the edge of the `view`.

**Content priorities.** A view with an intrinsic content size (label, button, image) knows the natural size it needs. Two priority values decide who gives way when space is short or left over, and each is set per axis: `label.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.required, for: .horizontal)` makes the label resist shrinking in width (the axis is `.horizontal` or `.vertical`), and `setContentHuggingPriority` controls resistance to growing. The view with the lower hugging is the one that stretches. The one with the lower compression resistance is cut first. Priorities range from 0 to 1000, and `.required` is 1000 (the mandatory constraint; below that, the system may break it).

**UIStackView.** It defines four properties: `axis` (direction, `.vertical` or `.horizontal`), `spacing` (space between items), `distribution` (how the space along the axis is divided, for example `.fillEqually`) and `alignment` (position on the perpendicular axis). Hiding an arranged subview (`isHidden = true`) removes it from the layout and the stack redistributes the space.

**Order and role of the lifecycle methods.** When the screen first appears: `viewDidLoad` (once, when the view was loaded), then `viewWillAppear` (before every appearance) and `viewDidAppear` (already visible). On the way out, `viewWillDisappear` runs right before (a good place to save drafts or stop timers). When you come back from a detail screen to a list, `viewWillAppear` runs again but `viewDidLoad` does not: that is why heavy loading goes in `viewDidLoad` and only the refresh of changed data goes in `viewWillAppear`. When overriding, call `super`: `override func viewWillAppear(_ animated: Bool) { super.viewWillAppear(animated) }`. Exception: if you override `loadView` to build the root view in code, assign `view = UIView()` and do not call `super.loadView()`.

**Stack or modal: each closes its own way.** A controller pushed with `navigationController?.pushViewController(detail, animated: true)` leaves with `popViewController(animated:)` (the navigation controller adds the Back button). A controller presented with `present(vc, animated: true)` is modal and leaves with `dismiss(animated: true)`; `pop` does not work on it. Modal styles: `fullScreen` covers everything, `pageSheet` and `formSheet` appear as a card. The bar title lives in each controller's `navigationItem.title`; the navigation controller shows the item of the one on top. A `UITabBarController` holds one controller per tab, and each tab can have its own `UINavigationController`.

**Passing data.** With a segue, the system calls `prepare(for:sender:)` just before the transition. `segue.destination` is of type `UIViewController`, so cast it to the expected class:
`override func prepare(for segue: UIStoryboardSegue, sender: Any?) {`
`if let destination = segue.destination as? DetailViewController { destination.order = order } }`
To trigger a segue from code: `performSegue(withIdentifier: "showDetail", sender: self)`. The 'show' segue pushes inside a navigation controller and presents modally outside one. Without a segue, create the controller by the Storyboard ID set in the Identity inspector: `storyboard?.instantiateViewController(withIdentifier: "Detail")`. To go back to a specific earlier controller, create an unwind segue (drag the button to Exit) tied to a method `@IBAction func backHere(_ segue: UIStoryboardSegue) { }` in the destination controller.

**Returning data: delegate.** Controller B declares a protocol and a property `weak var delegate: ChoiceDelegate?`; controller A adopts the protocol and assigns itself as the delegate. `weak` avoids a retain cycle between the two.

**Reused cells.** The table only creates the visible cells and recycles the ones that left the screen. That is why `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier: "Cell", for: indexPath)` returns an old cell, with its old content, and you must set every field on each call (including clearing the image). The identifier in code must be identical to the prototype cell's Reuse Identifier (without it, the crash is 'unable to dequeue a cell with identifier'). A `prepareForReuse()` in the cell subclass can also clear the content. On modern iOS, configure the text like this:
`var config = cell.defaultContentConfiguration()`
`config.text = items[indexPath.row]`
`cell.contentConfiguration = config`
(`textLabel` is deprecated). `indexPath` has `section` and `row` (in collections, `item`); use `items[indexPath.row]` to find the data.

**Sections and counts.** `numberOfSections(in:)` reports the number of sections (optional; the default is 1) and `numberOfRowsInSection` must return exactly `items.count`, never a fixed value, otherwise `cellForRowAt` accesses an index that does not exist ('index out of range'). `titleForHeaderInSection` gives each section a title.

**Animated updates and swipe.** After changing the array, `deleteRows(at: [indexPath], with: .automatic)` removes only those rows with animation, while `reloadData()` discards and recreates everything. If the data source's count does not match the changes, the app crashes. The 'Delete' button on swipe comes from the delegate method that returns the actions for the trailing side:
`func tableView(_ t: UITableView, trailingSwipeActionsConfigurationForRowAt indexPath: IndexPath) -> UISwipeActionsConfiguration? {`
`let delete = UIContextualAction(style: .destructive, title: "Delete") { _, _, done in items.remove(at: indexPath.row); t.deleteRows(at: [indexPath], with: .automatic); done(true) }`
`return UISwipeActionsConfiguration(actions: [delete]) }`

**Diffable data source.** Instead of counting rows, you describe the desired state with a snapshot and the system computes and animates the difference:
`var snapshot = NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<Int, String>()`
`snapshot.appendSections([0])`
`snapshot.appendItems(["a", "b"])`
`dataSource.apply(snapshot, animatingDifferences: true)`
First the sections (`appendSections`), then the items in them. Section and item types must be `Hashable`. This avoids the inconsistent-count crash.

**UICollectionView.** It is the table as a grid or free layout: it uses a data source and reusable cells like the table, but delegates positioning to a layout object. `UICollectionViewFlowLayout` covers simple grids and `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout` composes item, group and section (`NSCollectionLayoutItem`, `NSCollectionLayoutGroup`, `NSCollectionLayoutSection`).

**Target-action needs `@objc`.** `button.addTarget(self, action: #selector(tapped), for: .touchUpInside)` registers `self`'s `tapped` method for the event. `#selector` uses the Objective-C runtime, so the method must be exposed to it: `@objc func tapped() { }`. Without `@objc`, the compiler refuses. The most common event is `.touchUpInside`, fired when the finger lifts inside the button's bounds, which lets the user cancel by dragging out (`.touchDown` fires right at the touch, `.valueChanged` on controls such as switches and sliders).

**Delegate: protocol + weak reference.** A delegate is a contract (protocol) with several methods, and works one-to-one. For a `weak` property, the protocol must be class-constrained: `protocol ChoiceDelegate: AnyObject { func chose(_ item: String) }` and `weak var delegate: ChoiceDelegate?`. Assigning the property is what connects the two sides: `textField.delegate = self` makes the controller receive the field's events (for example `textFieldShouldReturn`), but only if it adopts `UITextFieldDelegate`; without the assignment, those methods are never called.

**NotificationCenter: one-to-many.** Define the name: `extension Notification.Name { static let scoreUpdated = Notification.Name("scoreUpdated") }`. The sender calls `NotificationCenter.default.post(name: .scoreUpdated, object: nil)` and whoever cares calls `addObserver(forName: .scoreUpdated, object: nil, queue: .main) { _ in ... }`, without the objects knowing each other. Keep the return value of `addObserver` and call `removeObserver` when needed.

**Hierarchy, frame and visibility.** Creating a view does not show it: `view.addSubview(label)` puts it in the hierarchy, and it needs a size (a `frame` such as `CGRect(x:y:width:height:)`, in the superview's coordinates, or constraints). With a zero `frame` and no constraints, it is invisible. `isHidden = true` hides the view (and removes it from the layout in a stack view); `alpha = 0` makes it transparent, but it still takes up space, and `alpha` can be animated. They are independent: `isHidden = true` followed by `alpha = 1` keeps the view hidden.

**Alerts.** `UIAlertController` is a view controller. Create it, add actions and present it: `let alert = UIAlertController(title: "Error", message: "Try again", preferredStyle: .alert)`, then `alert.addAction(UIAlertAction(title: "OK", style: .default))` and `present(alert, animated: true)`. `addSubview` is not the way.

**SwiftUI and UIKit together.** `UIHostingController(rootView: MyView())` puts SwiftUI inside UIKit. The opposite uses `UIViewRepresentable`, with two methods: `func makeUIView(context: Context) -> UILabel { UILabel() }` creates the view once and `func updateUIView(_ v: UILabel, context: Context) { v.text = "x" }` updates it when SwiftUI state changes. The `AppDelegate` handles the process and chooses the scene configuration; the `SceneDelegate` responds to each scene's lifecycle and holds its `UIWindow`.
